summary: Every rover, solar panel and battery is tested on Earth before it flies, but nobody says how much that test counts. Analog sites are usually ranked by how much they resemble the Moon or Mars, but hardware fails from accumulated damage, not from resemblance. We developed Analog Exchange Rate, an open web tool built on a new metric: k = damage of one year at the Earth site / damage of one year at the destination, so one year of testing here equals k years there. Using NASA POWER, LRO Diviner, Curiosity REMS and Perseverance MEDA, we computed k for 17,202 land cells on Earth against four destinations (lunar south pole and equator, Gale and Jezero craters) and four kinds of wear: thermal fatigue, deep cold, long night and dust. It addresses the challenge by naming the best Earth location for each wear and stating where the analogy breaks: vacuum, radiation and low gravity have no rate. Example: one year in the Altiplano of Nor Lípez equals 6 months of thermal fatigue at the Moon's south pole. It matters because Artemis and Mars teams can plan test campaigns in years of real exposure instead of similarity percentages.
details:
What it does

Analog Exchange Rate is a web page that tells you where on Earth to test Moon and Mars hardware, and how much one year of testing there really counts. You pick the hardware (rover, solar panel, battery or habitat) and the destination (lunar south pole, lunar equator, Gale crater or Jezero crater). The page returns the best place on Earth for each kind of wear, the exchange rate k, and what cannot be tested on Earth at all.

How it works

Analog studies usually score how much a place resembles the Moon or Mars. Hardware does not fail from resemblance: it fails from accumulated damage. So for each kind of wear we compute the same damage number D for one year at the Earth site and for one year at the destination, and divide:

k = D_here(1 year) / D_there(1 year)

  • 1 year of testing here = k years there
  • Thermal fatigue: D = sum of (daily ground temperature swing)^m over one year, with m from 2 to 3 (a Coffin-Manson type law, summed with Miner's rule).
  • Deep cold: hours per year below -40 °C.
  • Long night: the longest continuous darkness of the year (compared, not accumulated).
  • Dust: optical depth of mineral dust.
  • Vacuum, radiation and low gravity: the damage does not exist on Earth, so no rate exists. The page says so instead of giving a low score.

Data from three worlds

  • Earth: 17,202 land cells from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES, climatology 2001-2025), searched from coarse to fine: the whole globe every 2.5°, then every native cell (about 55 km) in the 49 best 10° zones.
  • Moon: 145 cells of the LRO Diviner global product, read from PDS by HTTP byte range (about 11 KB per cell instead of downloading 156 MB files).
  • Mars: 4,708 sols of ground temperature at Gale (Curiosity REMS) and 53 sampled sols at Jezero (Perseverance MEDA).

Click any point on the Earth map and the page asks NASA POWER for that exact point and computes the rate in the browser. Maps are live tiles from NASA GIBS and NASA Solar System Treks; the lunar polar relief comes from LRO LOLA.

The page has two linked tabs. Tab 1, Exchange rate, is the new metric: two maps at the same scale (destination and Earth site) with the factor k between them, and a side panel of ten sections, from the formula to the sources. Tab 2, Site atlas, is the usual similarity index (7 variables, 14 Earth sites against 4 lunar south pole sites and 4 Mars sites). Every site in the atlas links to its ex change rate, so the conventional view and the new metric can be compared side by side.

What we found

Rates at fatigue exponent m = 2.5.

  • Thermal fatigue: Altiplano of Nor Lípez, Bolivia-Chile border (21°S 68.13°W). One year there = 6 months at the lunar south pole (3 to 14 months depending on the material) and 5 weeks at Gale, Mars.
  • Deep cold: Dome Argus, Antarctica (80.5°S 78.75°E). One year there = 10 months at the lunar south pole and 20 months on Mars.
  • Dust: Kanem, Chad (15°N 14.4°E), downwind of the Bodélé Depression. One year there = 14 months on Mars.
  • Long night: South Pole. Its winter night lasts 12 lunar nights.
  • No single place wins twice: a full test campaign needs four sites on three continents, plus a chamber.
  • The famous analogs are not the best for wear: the place found by the search beats the best famous analog by 1.5x for thermal fatigue, 12.7x for dust and 16x for deep cold.

Earth is a slow test for thermal fatigue on Mars, and a good one for cold, darkness and dust.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Artemis and Mars teams can plan a test campaign in years of real exposure: which site retires which risk, and in how long.
  • The answer is given in time, not in a percentage, so it can go straight into a test plan and a mission length.
  • It says clearly where the analogy holds, where it is partial and where it breaks, which is what the challenge asks for.
  • Anyone can click their own town and see what a year there is worth on the Moon or Mars.
  • It is open source (MIT license) and a static page with no server of our own, so it is free to host, easy to audit and easy to reuse.

Tools, languages and software

  • Web page: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), Leaflet 1.9.4 for the maps, self-hosted fonts, no build step. Hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Data pipeline: nine Python 3 scripts (numpy, Pillow) that download the NASA products and build the page data.
  • Tests: 22 automated tests with the Node.js test runner, plus a Python check that every figure names a source and that every source link answers.
  • AI assistant: Claude (Anthropic) helped write and debug the code, extract the data, edit the text and prepare the slides. Every number is computed by the open formulas in the repository from NASA data; no image is AI-generated.
  • Code: https://github.com/chikiyu/analog-exchange-rate

How it is creative

  • It replaces the similarity score with an exchange rate, a metric we did not find in analog studies: the same damage number on both worlds, then one division.
  • It searches the whole planet instead of starting from a list of famous analog sites. The search knows no place names.
  • When a damage mechanism does not exist on Earth, the tool gives no rate instead of a low score. The limit of the analogy is part of the result.
  • It keeps the conventional similarity atlas beside the new metric, so the difference between "looks alike" and "is worth" is visible.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific validity
  • Reproducible: one script rebuilds every cell from the NASA files, byte for byte.
  • Traceable: every figure on the page carries a numbered link to its source.
  • Blind sanity check: without knowing any place name, the search lands on Dome Argus (the coldest region on Earth) and beside the Bodélé Depression (the largest dust source on Earth).
  • Two rovers agree: the ground swings 84.1 K a day at Gale and 80.3 K at Jezero.

Limits we state on the page

  • The fatigue rate changes about five-fold with the material exponent m, so the range for m = 2 to 3 is always shown.
  • Earth uses monthly means; damage is convex, so Earth is slightly understated.
  • Deep cold matches hours, not depth: -60 °C is not -200 °C.
  • The Mars dust level (optical depth 0.5) and our dust filter are our assumptions, and are labelled as such.
  • Earth cells are about 55 km wide. The REMS feed is an outreach product, and Jezero rests on 53 sampled sols.
  • The atlas uses 14 hand-picked Earth sites; it is not a global search.
  • Built by a team of two at the Arequipa local event, Peru.
